stories.title: Naftali Group Brings CorePower Yoga to Gramercy
stories.excerpt: Naftali Group said that CorePower Yoga, the nation’s largest yoga studio brand, will open at The Willow, Naftali’s new luxury residential development located at 201 E. 23rd St. in Manhattan’s Gramercy neighborhood. Marking CorePower Yoga’s first location in Gramercy, the forthcoming studio will bring a new wellness destination to the ground floor of the boutique-scale residential building, which recently opened to residents. “We are thrilled to welcome CorePower Yoga to The Willow,” said Danielle Naftali, EVP, Marketing, Sales and Design of Naftali Group. “The building was designed to feel deeply connected to Gramercy, with a strong sense of place that reflects the neighborhood’s history, character and daily rhythm. Bringing CorePower Yoga into that environment adds another thoughtful layer to the experience, introducing a wellness destination that complements both daily life at the project and the surrounding neighborhood.” The new CorePower Yoga location will occupy approximately 3,100 square feet of prime retail space along Third Avenue and 23rd Street. Slated to open towards the end of the year, the studio will further expand the brand’s New York City presence with its signature heated yoga, strength and recovery-focused classes, rooted in mindfulness and community connection. The post Naftali Group Brings CorePower Yoga to Gramercy appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Naftali Group opens CorePower Yoga at The Willow, 201 E. 23rd St., Gramercy, Manhattan.
3,100 SF ground-floor retail space leased; studio opens late 2024.
Wellness amenity signals luxury residential marketing focus on lifestyle integration.
stories.summary: Naftali Group has secured CorePower Yoga, the nation's largest yoga brand, as a ground-floor tenant at The Willow, its newly opened luxury residential tower in Gramercy. The 3,100 SF studio will occupy prime retail at Third Avenue and 23rd Street, opening by year-end. The lease reflects developer strategy to blend market-rate residential with high-end lifestyle anchors to justify premium pricing and differentiate boutique-scale luxury product.
stories.impact: Limited direct impact on multifamily development economics. The deal signals strong retail demand for wellness amenities in luxury Manhattan residential, which can support slightly higher rents and faster absorption—but this is a single-asset marketing tactic, not a market-wide supply or demand shift. Relevant to Gramercy repositioning trend only.

stories.title: 1031 Deadline Means Fast Closing on Lynwood Retail Center
stories.excerpt: Hanley Investment Group Real Estate Advisors represented the buyer in the acquisition of a Walgreens‑anchored, 39,146‑square‑foot center located at 10901–10927 Atlantic Ave. and 4351 E. Imperial Hwy. in Lynwood. The purchase price was $15 million. VP Ayda Kach represented the all-cash buyer, a longtime client and a privately held retail real estate investment firm and developer based in Los Angeles. The seller, The Bilak Companies of Beverly Hills, was represented by Newmark Retail Capital Markets, including Glenn Rudy, Rob Ippolito, and Pete Bethea. “Atlantic Crossing required a fast and disciplined effort to meet our client’s 1031 deadline, and we were able to complete the acquisition in 20 days,” said Kach. “Our team guided the buyer through a detailed due diligence process and kept the transaction moving efficiently from LOI through closing. The collaboration between all parties allowed us to deliver a smooth all‑cash closing on a strong, necessity‑based retail asset.” The post 1031 Deadline Means Fast Closing on Lynwood Retail Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Privately held LA retail investor acquired 39,146 SF Walgreens-anchored center in Lynwood for $15M.
All-cash deal closed in 20 days to meet 1031 exchange deadline.
Necessity-based retail asset with anchor tenant; tight timeline enabled transaction velocity.
stories.summary: Hanley Investment Group facilitated a $15 million all-cash sale of Atlantic Crossing, a 39,146 SF Walgreens-anchored retail center at 10901–10927 Atlantic Ave. and 4351 E. Imperial Hwy. in Lynwood, to a Los Angeles-based privately held retail investor. The transaction closed in just 20 days to satisfy the buyer's 1031 exchange deadline. The deal highlights demand for necessity-based, cash-flowing retail assets among 1031 investors seeking safe harbor for capital.
stories.impact: Minimal impact on multifamily development. The speed and all-cash nature reflect strong investor appetite for stabilized, necessity-anchored retail as a 1031 vehicle, not demand signals for residential. Lynwood retail market mechanics differ from residential. Not material to apartment development underwriting or acquisition strategy.

stories.title: Cord Meyer Breaks Ground on Rentals at Bay Terrace Shopping Center
stories.excerpt: Cord Meyer Development broke ground on its new residential community at the Bay Terrace Shopping Center, which the company developed more than 60 years ago. The $100-million-plus development will bring 145 new rental residences to Bayside in two five-story buildings being constructed on currently underutilized upper-level parking areas off 26th Avenue. “Cord Meyer has been part of Queens for more than 120 years, and we believe strongly in its future,” said Danielle Molaison, VP of Development at Cord Meyer Development. “One of the borough’s most pressing needs is additional housing, and we’re proud to help address that here in Bay Terrace. This is a community where people want to stay, and these new residences will provide more options for those who want to continue calling it home.” Callahan Construction Managers is serving as general contractor for the project. Callahan also serves as general contractor for 70 Westchester Avenue, Cord Meyer’s 203-unit residential development currently under construction in White Plains. The post Cord Meyer Breaks Ground on Rentals at Bay Terrace Shopping Center appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Cord Meyer breaks ground on 145-unit rental community at Bay Terrace Shopping Center, Bayside, Queens.
$100M+ development in two five-story buildings on underutilized parking areas off 26th Avenue.
Repurposing existing mixed-use asset to add housing; addresses Queens housing shortage.
stories.summary: Cord Meyer Development broke ground on a $100 million-plus residential project delivering 145 rental units in two five-story buildings at Bay Terrace Shopping Center in Bayside, Queens, where the developer has operated for over 120 years. The project converts underutilized upper-level parking into new housing, directly addressing one of the borough's acute housing shortages. Callahan Construction Managers is the GC; the developer is simultaneously building 203 units in White Plains.
stories.impact: Queens residential pipeline reinforcement. A 145-unit supply addition in Bayside—a historically underserved submarket with strong demographic fundamentals and transit access (26th Ave corridor)—will tighten competition for renters seeking value-oriented family housing. The adaptive-reuse strategy (parking-to-residential) is capital-efficient and signals developer confidence in Bayside demand. Relevant for Queens acquisition timing and competitive positioning; underscores inventory scarcity in outer boroughs.

stories.title: Private Investor Snags Brea Offices for $28M
stories.excerpt: CBRE facilitated the $27.8-million sale of Fairway Center II, a 135,308-square-foot office property located at 675 Placentia Ave. in Brea. CBRE represented the institutional seller. The Whittier Comstock, LLC, a subsidiary of MW Investment, LLC and owned by Matt Waken, acquired the property. CBRE’s Anthony DeLorenzo with National Office Properties, along with Sammy Cemo, Bryan Johnson and Jackson Marlow, represented the seller. Shaun Moothart and Andrew Post of CBRE’s Debt & Structured Finance practice secured the financing for the buyer. “Fairway Center II attracted significant interest amongst the investment and owner/user community alike,” said DeLorenzo. “We received multiple competitive offers from a variety of buyer profiles and awarded the property to a private investor within the first 30 days of marketing.” The property was 70.5% leased at the time of the sale. The property is anchored by the County of Orange, which occupies more than 61,000 square feet under a long-term lease. The post Private Investor Snags Brea Offices for $28M appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: MW Investment/Matt Waken acquired 135,308 SF Fairway Center II office in Brea for $27.8M.
Property 70.5% leased; anchored by County of Orange (61,000 SF, long-term lease).
Institutional seller; private investor acquired within 30 days of marketing; strong bidding interest.
stories.summary: CBRE brokered the $27.8 million sale of Fairway Center II, a 135,308 SF office property at 675 Placentia Ave. in Brea, to The Whittier Comstock, LLC (owned by Matt Waken), a private investor. The asset was 70.5% leased at sale, anchored by a long-term County of Orange lease occupying 61,000 SF. The property attracted multiple offers and closed within 30 days, signaling investor appetite for stabilized, government-anchored office assets.
stories.impact: Minimal impact on multifamily development. Orange County office sales do not signal residential demand or supply shifts. The government anchor and strong bidding reflect flight-to-quality in office markets, not residential market dynamics. Brea is not a major multifamily focus market for TCR. Not material.

stories.title: Vango Development Launches Leasing at Third Rutherford-Area Property
stories.excerpt: Vango Development has launched leasing at Parker East, a new five-story luxury rental community bringing 86 residences, indoor and outdoor lifestyle amenities and convenient mass-transit access to 263 Hackensack St. in East Rutherford, NJ. Located 0.2 miles from the Rutherford NJ TRANSIT station, Parker East offers one- and two-bedroom residences priced from $3,250. Immediate occupancy is available. The Taylor Lucyk Group is serving as the community’s exclusive leasing agent. “Parker East reflects our continued commitment to creating high-quality residential communities in well-connected neighborhoods,” said Van Golemis, CEO of Vango Development. “The combination of spacious residences, a strong amenity offering and a location close to both transit and Rutherford’s downtown gives residents the convenience and connectivity they’re looking for today.” The property is the latest addition to Vango’s growing portfolio in the area, following the development and lease-up of Parker 106 and Parker 118 in neighboring Rutherford. The post Vango Development Launches Leasing at Third Rutherford-Area Property appeared first on Connect CRE.
bullets: Vango Development launches leasing at Parker East, 86-unit luxury rental in East Rutherford, NJ.
Five-story building at 263 Hackensack St., 0.2 miles from NJ TRANSIT Rutherford station; units from $3,250.
Third Vango project in Rutherford area following Parker 106 and Parker 118; immediate occupancy available.
stories.summary: Vango Development has opened leasing at Parker East, an 86-unit luxury rental community in East Rutherford, NJ, located just 0.2 miles from the Rutherford NJ TRANSIT station. Units are priced from $3,250 for one- and two-bedroom configurations, with immediate occupancy. This is Vango's third project in the Rutherford submarket, following Parker 106 and Parker 118, demonstrating developer confidence and repeat-market validation.
stories.impact: East Rutherford/Hudson County transit-oriented rental momentum. Three Vango deliveries in the same micro-market signals strong absorption and developer confidence in transit-proximate rents ($3,250+ for two-BR in Rutherford suggests pricing power via NJ TRANSIT access and NYC connectivity). The submarket is tightening competitively; future entrants should model peer pricing and occupancy momentum. Relevant for North Jersey acquisition strategy and rent-growth benchmarking.

stories.title: CIBC Supplies $102M Refi for SkyREM Industrial Portfolio
stories.excerpt: Real estate investment firm SkyREM has secured $101.8 million to refinance a 1.9 million-square-foot industrial portfolio across the East Coast, Commercial Observer has learned. CIBC provided the nonrecourse financing, which carries an initial three-year term with two one-year extension options. JLL Capital Markets’ Peter Rotchford, Steven Binswanger and Lucas Borges arranged the transaction on behalf of SkyREM. “This financing reflects the strength of the portfolio and gives us additional flexibility to continue investing in well-located industrial assets where we see compelling long-term value,” SkyREM CEO Alexander Dembitzer said in a statement. The industrial portfolio spans four properties and is 100 percent occupied by six tenants, according to JLL. The East Coast properties, located in Georgia, Florida, and South Carolina, serve a range of warehousing, manufacturing and e-commerce uses. SkyREM, which holds dual offices in New York City and Philadelphia, owns and operates 30 properties across a largely industrial U.S. portfolio, according to its website. The firm counts Lockheed Martin, FedEx, Amazon and Shein among its major tenants. SkyREM most recently acquired a 325,334-square-foot manufacturing facility in Casa Grand, Ariz., according to a January release. In early 2025, the firm secured a $170 million refinancing for a 10-building, 2.5 million-square-foot portfolio. That loan was provided by affiliates of Apollo, and was also arranged by JLL. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: CIBC refinances $101.8M for SkyREM industrial portfolio; 1.9M SF across East Coast.
Four properties in Georgia, Florida, South Carolina; 100% occupied by six tenants.
Three-year term plus two one-year extensions; nonrecourse structure; JLL arranged transaction.
stories.summary: SkyREM secured $101.8 million in nonrecourse financing from CIBC to refinance a 1.9 million SF industrial portfolio spanning four properties in Georgia, Florida, and South Carolina. The portfolio is 100% occupied across warehousing, manufacturing, and e-commerce uses. The financing carries a three-year initial term with two one-year extension options, arranged by JLL. The deal reflects investor confidence in East Coast industrial fundamentals despite rising rates.
stories.impact: Industrial capital availability signal, not direct multifamily impact. The successful refi of a fully leased, diversified industrial portfolio indicates lender appetite for essential-use real estate and East Coast logistics demand. This indirectly signals regional economic resilience and supply-chain investment in the Sunbelt—positive for concurrent multifamily demand in GA, FL, SC submarkets driven by industrial job growth. Useful for regional demand underwriting, not for development capital availability.

stories.title: As Fed Hikes Rates for First Time Since 2023, Commercial Real Estate Comes to Terms
stories.excerpt: The Federal Reserve raised interest rates for the first time in more than three years Wednesday, but the hawkish move is not expected to curtail commercial real estate transactions in the latter half of 2026. In a unanimous 12-0 vote, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) hiked its benchmark interest rate a quarter point to between 3.75 percent and 4 percent, noting continued inflationary pressures that have been compounded by the war in Iran. The move followed five straight rate holds and marked the central bank’s first time increasing borrowing costs since July 2023. The Fed also released its updated quarterly “dot plot” matrix of individual committee members, which signaled an additional rate hike later this year would likely be supported by 16 of 18 FOMC participants. Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has not participated in the dot plot exercise since taking over the leadership post in June. “The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long,” Warsh said in a post-meeting press conference. “This summer’s inflation readings do not tell me that underlying trends have meaningfully improved.” The FOMC said it remains committed to maintaining the board’s long-standing inflation goal of a 2 percent annual rate, and that recent data put the rate well above this target. The Fed’s dot plot grid projected the federal funds rate at 4.1 percent for the end of 2026 and remain at that level through 2027. Since assuming the Fed chair post from Jerome Powell, Warsh has presided over two pauses and one rate hike in his first three meetings as Fed chair despite external pressure from President Donald Trump, who nominated Warsh in January. In a Sept. 4 Truth Social post, Trump called on the Fed to cut interest rates or he would stop trading with certain countries. bullets: Federal Reserve raises benchmark rate 25 bps to 3.75–4.00%, first hike since July 2023.
16 of 18 FOMC dot-plot participants signal additional hike likely later in 2026.
Rate cycle resumption cited as inflationary pressures, Iran war spillovers; CRE transaction velocity expected to hold.
stories.summary: The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate a quarter point to 3.75–4.00% in a unanimous FOMC vote, marking the first rate increase since July 2023. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh cited persistent inflation and geopolitical pressures (Iran war). The dot plot indicated 16 of 18 committee members likely favor an additional rate hike later in 2026. Despite the hawkish move, analysts do not expect near-term disruption to commercial real estate transaction volume in the latter half of 2026.
stories.impact: CRITICAL for multifamily capital and underwriting. Rate hikes directly compress cap rates, increase debt-service costs on construction financing and permanent loans, and reduce acquisition pricing power. With SOFR rising and additional hikes signaled, floating-rate construction loans (standard for development) will see higher carrying costs mid-build. Development feasibility thresholds tighten; underwriting IRR and exit assumptions must absorb higher refinance rates. Affects deal spreads and site valuation across all major markets. Tighten leverage assumptions and lengthen hold timelines in 2026 acquisitions.

stories.title: Law Firm Greenberg Traurig Expands to 133K SF at One Vanderbilt
stories.excerpt: Law firm Greenberg Traurig has no objections to its Midtown offices at One Vanderbilt — in fact, it’s taking even more space there. The law firm, which provides legal services to businesses, financial institutions and high-profile individuals, has signed a 10.5-year lease for 33,477 additional square feet on the entire 33rd floor of SL Green Realty’s trophy high-rise at 1 Vanderbilt Avenue, according to the landlord. The lease brings Greenberg’s total office footprint at the skyscraper to 133,365 square feet. Greenberg signed its initial 15-year lease for four contiguous floors at One Vanderbilt in January 2018, before the 1.7 million-square-foot office tower was completed in 2020. The law firm moved from its previous offices at the MetLife Building at 200 Park Avenue, where its lease expired in 2021. The asking rent for the firm’s new expansion lease at One Vanderbilt was not disclosed, but Steven Durels, executive vice president and director of leasing and real property at SL Green, told Commercial Observer in February that rents in the building range from between $250 to “well over $300” per square foot. “Strong leasing momentum continues unabated with many tenants expanding and making significant capital investment to provide upscale work environments to better recruit and retain employee talent,” Durels said in a statement. CBRE’s Michael Monahan and Mark Ravesloot brokered the deal for Greenberg, while it’s unclear whether SL Green had any representation. Spokespeople for CBRE and Greenberg did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Greenberg’s expansion keeps One Vanderbilt at 100 percent leased. Other office tenants include TD Bank, investment management firm Carlyle Group, alternative investment firm Oak Hill Advisors and SL Green itself. News of the deal also comes during a recent wave of office leasing for SL Green, which said it has signed 129 office leases in Manhattan totaling 1.8 million square feet so far in 2026. bullets: Greenberg Traurig expands by 33,477 SF at One Vanderbilt, SL Green office tower in Midtown.
Total lease footprint now 133,365 SF on entire 33rd floor; 10.5-year term signed.
Firm vacated MetLife Building (200 Park Avenue) in 2021; original One Vanderbilt lease signed January 2018.

The lease covers the entire 33rd floor. Greenberg originally signed a 15-year lease for four contiguous floors in January 2018 before the 1.7M SF tower opened in 2020, having vacated its MetLife Building space in 2021. Asking rents at One Vanderbilt remain in the disclosed range but were not specified for this lease.
stories.impact: Midtown office durability signal, not residential impact. A major law firm committing 10+ years and expanding footprint at One Vanderbilt is a positive for NYC office recovery narrative, but does not indicate residential demand shifts. Law firm consolidation in trophy assets reflects flight-to-quality and prestige (not demand elasticity). Irrelevant to multifamily supply, demand, or capital dynamics.

stories.title: In Pro-Development South Florida, NIMBYism Rises
stories.excerpt: When Catherine Adler first moved to the West Palm Beach area in 1991, the South Florida city counted only a handful of high-rises, most of which were clustered around downtown. Today, though, she barely recognizes the regional city. Since 2019, at least nine towers have been completed. More than 10 are now under construction, some rising in residential neighborhoods packed with single-family homes. And more change is likely to come: Another nine developments have already been approved. “There’s cranes everywhere. You turn around and, all of a sudden, something’s going up,” Adler said. “The beautiful waterfront, the historic neighborhoods, and the charm — I don’t know if that’s going to be around.” South Florida has long been a bastion of new development. For decades, the region prospered thanks to pro-development policies that fueled a boom in condominium construction that attracted vacationers, retirees, foreign investors looking for a second home and wealthy newcomers. But, in recent years, South Florida has faced an all-too familiar obstacle: NIMBYism. The “Not In My Back Yard” phenomenon has long been common in places with starkly different politics, such as New York and California, but after years of developer free-for-all, NIMBYism has now finally descended onto South Florida. “We might be reaching a turning point,” said David Foster, an assistant professor at Florida State University who studies the politics of housing. “There’s nothing inherently partisan or conservative or liberal necessarily about homeowners’ opposition to development.” While South Florida, like most regions, has had its share of NIMBYism over the years, the movement is gaining significant steam since the COVID-19 pandemic, when millions of Northeasterners moved south to Florida. bullets: South Florida NIMBYism rising despite pro-development history: 9 towers completed since 2019, 10+ under construction.
West Palm Beach single-family neighborhoods now host residential high-rises; 9 additional projects approved.
Historic charm and neighborhood character concerns emerging among longtime residents; regulatory friction increasing.
stories.summary: South Florida, long a pro-development bastion, is experiencing a surge in NIMBY opposition as residential density accelerates. Since 2019, nine towers have opened in West Palm Beach, with more than 10 under construction and nine additional projects approved. High-rise development now encroaches on traditionally single-family neighborhoods, prompting resident concerns about character loss, infrastructure strain, and waterfront impacts. The region's decades-long deregulatory advantage is eroding as growth itself triggers community backlash.
stories.impact: CRITICAL entitlement and feasibility risk for South Florida multifamily developers. Nascent NIMBYism signals regulatory capture and approval-timeline uncertainty ahead. Constituencies that enabled rapid-fire condo development are now organized and vocal; future projects in West Palm Beach, Boca Raton, and inner-ring Broward suburbs face longer entitlements, design demands, and mitigation costs. Land acquisition underwriting must factor increasing soft-cost risk and approval delays. Window for streamlined permitting is closing—prioritize shovel-ready sites and land-trust relationships now.

stories.title: George Soros Puts Argonaut Building on the Market for Roughly $100M
stories.excerpt: Another Manhattan office building has hit the market. This time it’s the landmarked Argonaut Building, an approximately 140,000-square-foot office and retail building at 224 West 57th Street in Midtown. George Soros’s Soros Fund Management has put the property up for sale and is seeking a price of roughly $100 million, according to a source with knowledge of the deal. The 1909-built building between Broadway and Seventh Avenue seems to be fully occupied by Soros’s grant-making group the Open Society Foundations, which moved into the building in 2013 and has a lease running through 2042. TD Bank is a retail tenant on the ground floor. In April 2024, Soros, as a tenant, filed a foreclosure lawsuit against former landlord eretz group citing a default on a $145 million mortgage, The Real Deal reported at the time. Eretz had purchased the site for $213.8 million in 2015. It’s unclear why Soros is now looking to offload the property after winning it in a foreclosure auction, but the billionaire plans to move his grant-making group from the building once a deal is closed, according to TRD, which first reported the listing news. Newmark’s Adam Spies, Adam Doneger and Willis Robbins are marketing the building. An offering memo from the brokerage said the sale is a “rare opportunity” to reposition the historic building into “best-in-class residences,” TRD reported. The property has additional air rights that could give it a total buildable space of more than 200,000 square feet, according to the publication. If an office-to-residential conversion does proceed at the West 57th Street building, it would join another conversion project nearby at 135 East 57th Street, where TF Cornerstone is turning the former office building into 350 apartments. Newmark declined to comment, while a spokesperson for Open Society Foundations did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Isabelle Durso can be reached at idurso@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: George Soros markets Argonaut Building, 224 W. 57th St., Manhattan for roughly $100M.
140,000 SF landmarked office/retail; fully leased to Open Society Foundations through 2042; TD Bank ground-floor retail.
Soros acquired asset in 2024 foreclosure auction; OSF relocation planned post-sale.
stories.summary: George Soros's Soros Fund Management has put the landmarked Argonaut Building (224 West 57th Street, Midtown Manhattan) on the market seeking approximately $100 million. The 140,000 SF office and retail property is fully occupied by the Open Society Foundations (which moved in 2013 under a lease running through 2042) and TD Bank retail. Soros acquired the asset in a 2024 foreclosure auction following a default on the prior owner's $145 million mortgage. The billionaire plans to relocate OSF once the property sells.
stories.impact: Minimal direct multifamily impact. A midtown office sale by a nonprofit tenant (OSF) does not signal residential demand, supply, or capital availability shifts. The $100M ask on 140K SF (~$714/SF) reflects Manhattan office distress, not residential market strength. Landmark status limits adaptive conversion viability. Not material to multifamily development strategy.
